audio_caption: The clip begins with a male speaker introducing a reaction and giving a shoutout to someone who recommended it. He notes that the reaction uses less dry chlorine and a shorter chlorination time, but requires hexamine, which might be an uncommon reagent in the US. He mentions buying hexamine tablets from army shops or a survival store, unsure if army shops are common in the US. He adds that, after the fact, he discovered the tablets contained trioxane.

The clip features a single male speaker discussing hexamine data, noting its low solubility in various solvents, particularly acetone. He describes measuring and dissolving tablets in water, heating them on a hotplate, and decanting the solution, revealing some junk in the tablets that he describes as possibly sand. Then he details adding 75 milliliters of benzyl chloride to the hexamine solution. In the background are soft bubbling sounds.

The clip begins with a statement, "Then start stirring and reflux for a few hours," spoken in a clear, instructive tone. Following this is the sound of bubbling water, suggesting a scientific or culinary context. A single speaker, male, describes observing changes as the water reached its boiling point, noting increased intensity but nothing alarming, conveying a calm and observational tone.

After things "calmed down a little bit", you could see "distinct layers", and over about 40 minutes, the "aqueous layer went from milky color to clear". Nothing exciting happened, and when the speaker returned after several hours, the "organic layer looked red", and the "aqueous layer started to look milky again". There were also "some crystals in the condenser", likely hexamine because "initially when the thing erupted a little bit" it threw vapor up there. All of this is delivered by a male speaker in a somewhat detached tone. Additionally, sounds of stirring are present in the background.

The audio clip begins with a male speaker explaining he is separating the organic layer, noting this step isn't strictly necessary but done due to available equipment and the need to neutralize amines, adding hydrochloric acid. He speaks in a factual, informative tone. He mentions the presence of benzoyl chloride, but in an unknown concentration.

The audio clip begins with a male speaker describing an "organic layer," noting its composition of "benzaldehyde," "methylamine," and "benzal chloride." His tone is informative and slightly technical. He suggests using hydrochloric acid to form a salt with methylamine that can be washed away with water and to hydrolyze the benzal chloride.

The clip begins with a male speaker talking about adding hydrochloric acid and observing a reaction that forms a thick fog, which he plans to reflux and distill off the benzaldehyde. He then states he has decided to distill benzaldehyde immediately with all its impurities. He justifies this decision by saying it is not bad because it will lead to a clear product, meaning, not yellow, and this will allow him to see what happens.

A male speaker begins, remarking about losing one-third of the product after distillation, specifying around "25 milliliters" which he judges acceptable considering the four-hour reflux in the atmosphere. He observes a color change within the first 30 minutes, and notes that after four hours the product "looks fairly processed," hoping for no impurities post-distillation. The speaker states he will separate the organic layer and then add a bunch of clean water. He mentions needing to neutralize hydrochloric acid, using calcium carbonate due to a lack of alternatives, figuring it works so "why not," right? The speaker concludes by announcing he is distilling the benzaldehyde.

The audio clip begins with a male speaker discussing a sample he distilled, mentioning putting it in a machine for analysis. He describes the taste and smell as very spicy, not aromatic, and notes the presence of benzaldehyde along with an overwhelming impurity he can't get rid of.

The clip starts with one male speaker discussing separating benzaldehyde and noting that there's less of it than initially. He mentions drying the benzaldehyde with calcium sulfate and regrets forgetting to dry his bottle beforehand. He then announces he obtained about 18 milliliters of benzaldehyde. A brief sound occurs at the end of the audio.

The audio begins with a male speaker who believes a certain method isn't bad, "this method sucks," because he did it on purpose to see if he could rid an impurity from the sample, but "unfortunately, I can't." The speaker speaks conversationally.

A single male speaker begins by stating he put benzaldehyde in the freezer to see if crystals would form, and that crystals did form. He mentions the temperature and states that it is not benzoic acid or benzoyl chloride, as it smells just like the benzaldehyde sample itself. He then notes that after filtering these crystals, the benzaldehyde smell was "really just awful," and "wasn't good at all."

A man is speaking in a factual and slightly surprised tone about a chemical process he's been doing, including "freezing and filtering." He notes that when he checked the graduated cylinder, he observed "crystals," and that there's "no liquid there." He concludes by stating, with a slightly impressed tone, that the "oxidation rate is quite impressive."

A single male speaker with a somewhat discouraged tone states that "vacuum distillation" did not remove an impurity, expressing disappointment that he cannot "present you a process that works perfectly well." He hopes that maybe he'll succeed on the sixth try, but he's unsure. He then states "here's the video of what I have now." He then concludes by saying "so, this is about everything I have for now, so see you later."
